topic: rebuilding a drystone dyke: foundation trench, hearting, throughbands and a tight cope

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-6)
provenance.notes: pisane niezaleznie, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: poziomica laserowa ustawiona na koncu odcinka

base: I have started rebuilding the drystone dyke along the top field and the first stretch keeps slumping.
The garden wall behind the house was built by my grandfather and has not moved in sixty years.
A laser level stands at the end of the run and gives me the line every morning.
I laid the foundation stones straight onto the turf and worked up from there with whatever came to hand.
Should the foundation go into a dug trench, or is laying it on firm turf good enough?
Dig the trench, because a dyke laid on turf will settle unevenly in the first winter it stands.
Take out the soft top until you reach firm ground, which is rarely more than a spade deep.
Set your largest stones as the foundation and bed each one until it cannot rock at all.
Every stone above copies the fault of the one beneath, so the bottom course decides everything.
I dug the trench out to firm ground and bedded the foundation stones so that none of them rock.
The laser level shows the line running true, yet the sides of the dyke lean out as I build.
I have been filling the middle with small stones and rubble because the faces take up so little room.
Is that hearting the cause of the lean, or am I setting the face stones badly?
The hearting is the cause, since loose rubble in the middle pushes the two faces steadily apart.
Pack the hearting by hand, stone against stone, and never shovel it in like so much gravel.
Each face stone should slope a little into the heart, so its weight leans inward rather than out.
Build both faces together, course by course, and check the batter with a frame as you go.
I packed the hearting by hand and made a batter frame out of three battens nailed together.
The faces now lean inward properly and the dyke has stopped spreading as it rises.
The garden wall has the very same inward lean, which I had never once noticed before.
I am about halfway up now and wondering when the long throughbands ought to go in.
Do they all go at one height, or spread through the dyke wherever they happen to fit?
Throughbands go in one continuous course at about two thirds of the height, not scattered about.
They must reach right across and show their ends on both faces, or they do no work at all.
A dyke without them can split down the middle and shed one whole face in a wet winter.
Set them level and bed them well, because everything above rides on that single course.
Above the throughbands the stone gets smaller, which makes the last courses quicker than the first.
The throughbands are in and they show on both faces along the whole length of the stretch.
I have reached the height where the cope should go and my stones vary a good deal.
Some are tall and thin while others are squat and would sit lower than their neighbours.
Should I sort them by height, or is an uneven top part of how these dykes look?
Sort them, but sort by thickness rather than height, since the cope must stand tight against itself.
Each cope stone leans on the next, so a thin one among thick ones will leave a gap.
Keep the tops roughly even and let the bottoms sit wherever the head of the wall allows.
A loose cope is how a dyke starts to come down, because sheep and frost work at the gaps.
I sorted the copes by thickness and set them tight, wedging the odd one with a small pin.
The finished stretch has stood through two months of rain without a single stone shifting.
Next spring I want to take down and rebuild the leaning stretch nearer the gate.
Is there any way to save the old stone, or does most of it get sorted out?
Almost all of it can be used again, since only frost shattered stone is truly finished.
Take the dyke down into three heaps, keeping face stones, throughbands and hearting apart.
Sorting as you strip saves more time than any other habit in the whole of the trade.
Then rebuild from the trench upward, and the stretch will outlast anything you set on turf.
